sail-01.title: Safety before speed
concepts: A good departure begins with the crew, weather, and boat, not the throttle. Wear a correctly fitted lifejacket, identify emergency equipment, and agree how to call for help and recover a person from the water.

Brief everyone on the boom, trip hazards, safe handholds, and keeping hands clear of loaded lines and winches. Check the forecast, local restrictions, communications, fuel or battery supply, and that the boat is seaworthy.

Choose conditions appropriate to the least experienced crew member and agree an abort plan. This course develops understanding and selected simulated skills; completion is not a qualification to skipper a real yacht.
observe: Before departure, tell your crew where to sit, how to move, and who will keep lookout.
Identify the boom and imagine its sweep across the cockpit.
sail-01.mistake: Starting because the weather looks pleasant without checking the forecast or briefing the crew.

quiz.prompt: A new crew member is aboard. What comes before departure?
options: Fit lifejackets and explain hazards, emergency equipment, and roles
Leave first and explain the controls underway
quiz.explanation: Prepare the crew and boat before getting underway; discovering a missing safety item after departure is too late.

quiz.prompt: What does passing this simulator course establish?
options: Understanding and selected skills in a simplified simulation
Readiness to sail alone in all weather
quiz.explanation: On-water instruction and assessment are still needed. The simulator omits many physical and environmental demands.

sail-01.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-02.title: Know your yacht
concepts: Bow means the front; stern means the back. Port is the left side and starboard the right when facing the bow. These names stay with the boat when you turn around.
The mainsail is behind the mast; the headsail is forward. The boom supports the mainsail foot. The keel contributes stability and resists sideways motion; the rudder steers when water flows over it.
Use Chase for the whole boat, Helm for the sailing viewpoint, and Cockpit to inspect the wheel, winches, and screens.
observe: Switch to Cockpit and locate the wheel, companionway, and sheet winches.
Switch to Chase and identify the bow, mast, boom, and two sails.
sail-02.mistake: Calling a side port or starboard from whichever direction you happen to be looking.

quiz.prompt: You are facing the stern. Which side is port?
options: Whichever side the wind comes from
quiz.explanation: Port is the yacht’s left when facing forward, so it is on your right when facing aft.

quiz.prompt: What needs water flowing over it to steer effectively?
quiz.explanation: The rudder changes the direction of water flow. With little boat speed its authority is reduced.

sail-02.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-03.title: Lines, winches, and loads
concepts: A halyard raises a sail. A sheet adjusts its angle. A reef reduces exposed sail area. A cleat or clutch holds a line; a winch helps manage load.

On this yacht, colored sheets run aft toward the cockpit winches. Inspect the wraps and clutches in Cockpit view. The Boat systems panel controls the two halyards and sheets independently, plus traveler, vang, outhaul, reefs, engine, and anchor rode. The sliders represent control settings, not physical line handling.

The main and headsail hoists set how much sail is exposed. The two sheets change sail angle independently. The traveler moves the boom’s sheeting position; vang tension controls modeled twist, while the outhaul flattens the modeled sail foot. Change one control at a time and compare the response.

Reef level reduces mainsail area. Engine throttle selects reverse, neutral, or ahead; return to neutral for sailing assessments. The anchor rode slider sets a target. Run the windlass to pay out or retrieve line over time; watch actual paid-out rode and stop the windlass when needed.
Keep fingers, loose clothing, and hair clear of loaded lines. Learn real winch loading, line handling, knots, and controlled easing with an instructor; a mouse cannot teach the feel of a loaded line.
observe: Follow a colored sheet from the deck toward its winch.
Compare a halyard’s lifting purpose with a sheet’s trimming purpose.
sail-03.mistake: Treating a heavily loaded sheet like an unloaded rope, or confusing the sheet with the halyard.

quiz.prompt: You want to adjust the mainsail’s angle. Which line has that job?
quiz.explanation: The mainsheet controls the boom and mainsail angle; the halyard hoists the sail.

quiz.prompt: Can the visual winch model assess safe handling of a loaded rope?
options: No; physical line handling needs supervised practice
quiz.explanation: The rendered hardware provides orientation, not a simulation of hand placement, friction, or line loads.

sail-03.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-04.title: Read the instruments
concepts: Heading is the direction the bow points, measured clockwise from north: 000° north, 090° east, 180° south, 270° west. Speed is shown in knots; one knot is one nautical mile per hour.

The multifunction display behind the wheel and the dashboard below the controls show the same live readings. Wind over water names where the wind comes from relative to moving water; its angle is measured from the bow. Depth estimates water depth, not clearance below the keel.

Current and leeway can make course over ground differ from heading, and speed over ground differ from speed through water. Compare these readings on the dashboard. You can enlarge the display for easier reading.

The app combines a compass and a wind indicator in one dial. North stays at the top, east at the right, south at the bottom, and west at the left, even when the boat or camera turns. Read the white boat symbol’s bow against the compass scale to find your heading.

The gold arrow identifies where wind over water comes from. The shaded no-go sector surrounds that source; it marks headings too close to the wind for sailing. In this example, the white boat points northeast at 045°, while the arrow and sector face northwest at 315°. The knots reading beneath the dial is wind speed.
observe: Open Helm or Cockpit and compare the multifunction display behind the wheel with the dashboard below the controls.
Select Chart and find the yacht symbol and north arrow.
Find the floating compass. Identify north, read the white boat’s heading, then read the gold wind-from arrow. These are two separate bearings.
sail-04.mistake: Reading depth as guaranteed clearance or treating heading as a guaranteed ground track.

quiz.prompt: Which heading points east?
quiz.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north; east is 090°.

quiz.prompt: At 6 knots, how far would you travel in 30 minutes without current?
quiz.explanation: Distance = speed × time. Six nautical miles per hour for half an hour is three nautical miles.

quiz.prompt: On the illustrated app compass, the white bow points to 045° and the gold arrow to 315°. What is your heading?
quiz.explanation: Heading comes from the white boat’s bow: 045°. The gold arrow gives the wind-from bearing, 315°. Neither the wind pointer nor the shaded sector is a course to follow.

sail-04.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Inspect the cockpit instruments
Open the navigation chart

practice.debrief: You can now locate the displays. Check instruments regularly while maintaining an outside lookout.

sail-05.title: Where the wind comes from
concepts: Wind is named for where it comes from. A northwesterly wind comes from the northwest (315°) and blows toward the southeast (135°). Windward is the side the wind comes from; leeward is the side it blows toward. Sailors name the source because that is where the wind’s force, the waves and any approaching weather come from.

A sail is a flexible wing: it only works when air flows across it at an angle. Point the bow straight into the wind and the sail lines up with the airflow and just flaps like a flag, so it makes no driving force. The no-go zone is the range of headings too close to the wind for the sail to work: about 40–45° on either side for most cruising yachts, and 38° in this simulator. To reach a place upwind, you sail a zigzag outside it.

The wind you sail by is the wind over the water. If the water itself is moving (a current), that wind differs from the weather report, which describes wind over the land. Once the boat moves, it also feels its own airflow, called apparent wind (Lesson 17). With no current, the forecast wind is the one that matters.

The app’s compass shows the wind like a weather vane: the gold arrowhead points to where the wind comes from, and the shaded no-go sector sits around it. Diagrams of moving air point the other way, toward where the air goes. In the example, wind from 315° and a heading of 045° are 90° apart: a beam reach. When the boat turns, only the white boat symbol moves; the gold arrow and the sector stay where the wind is.
observe: With no current and wind from 315°, compare headings 315°, 045°, and 135° on the compass.
The 045° heading puts the wind approximately across the side.
On the app compass, compare the white bow with the shaded sector. Say where the wind comes from and where the air moves before choosing a heading.
sail-05.mistake: Interpreting the arrow as where the wind is going rather than where it comes from.

quiz.prompt: A wind from 315° comes from which direction?
quiz.explanation: 315° is northwest. Wind direction is conventionally named for its source.

quiz.prompt: Why can a yacht not sail straight into the wind?
options: The sail lines up with the airflow and just flaps, so it makes no driving force
quiz.explanation: A sail needs air flowing across it at an angle. Outside the no-go zone it works like a wing; to go upwind you zigzag by tacking.

quiz.prompt: Why do the app’s gold arrow and shaded no-go sector both face 315° in this example?
options: They tell you to steer toward 315°
Both identify the wind’s source; the air moves toward 135°
quiz.explanation: The pointer marks wind from 315°, and the sector marks headings too close to that source. Air flows toward 135°. The white boat at 045° is outside the sector, on a beam reach.

sail-05.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-06.title: Raise the sails
concepts: Hoist the mainsail with the bow pointing into the wind. The sail then lines up with the airflow and flaps with almost no load (it luffs), so it slides up easily and the boom cannot swing hard. With the sheet eased, the sail cannot fill by surprise.

Before hoisting, check that halyards and sheets are clear and not twisted, that you have room to drift, and that the crew is clear of the boom. The mainsail usually goes up first: it sits at the back of the boat, so like the tail of a weather vane it helps hold the bow toward the wind while you work. The headsail follows. In the app, Raise sails hoists both at once; Boat systems hoists each one separately.
A raised sail facing the wind still makes no drive. To get moving, bear away until the wind is well to one side, then sheet in until the sails stop flapping. Only then do they work as wings.
observe: Start the exercise facing into the wind with sails lowered.
Raise the sails; then turn to a sailable course in later exercises.
sail-06.mistake: Assuming raised sails always propel the boat, or hoisting without first checking the lines and boom area.

quiz.prompt: Before a real mainsail hoist, what should be checked?
options: Clear lines, sea room, crew, and an unloaded sail
Whether the boat is at top speed
quiz.explanation: Preparation prevents jams and unexpected sail loading.

quiz.prompt: Why is the mainsail hoisted with the bow pointing into the wind?
options: The sail flaps with almost no load, so it goes up easily and the boom stays quiet
It makes the boat go fastest
quiz.explanation: Pointing into the wind, the sail lines up with the airflow and carries little load. Across the wind it would fill, pull hard and swing the boom while you are still hoisting.

sail-06.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Raise the sails

practice.debrief: You set the sails in the model. The next exercise starts on a reach where they can produce drive.

sail-07.title: Feel the boat accelerate
concepts: A beam reach puts the wind at about 90° to the boat. It is the easiest point of sail to start on: you are far from the no-go zone, and the sail can be set at a clear angle to the wind, so it makes plenty of forward drive.

A yacht weighs several tonnes, so it speeds up slowly. Water drag also grows quickly with speed. The boat accelerates until the push from the sails equals the drag from the water, then settles at a steady speed. Change the wind or the trim and it finds a new balance, again gradually.

The rudder is a small underwater wing. It only steers when water flows past it, so it does little at rest and grips better as speed builds; use small helm movements. A wheel steers like a car: turn it to port and the bow goes to port. A tiller works the opposite way: push it to starboard to turn the bow to port. If the boat ever moves backward, water reaches the rudder from behind and the same helm turns the bow the other way.
observe: Begin on 045° with a northwesterly wind, sails lowered, and anchor up.
Raise both sails, then watch speed increase. Keep the helm centered while the yacht builds steerage.
sail-07.mistake: Applying full helm while stationary and expecting the yacht to pivot instantly.

quiz.prompt: When does this rudder gain steering authority?
options: As water flow and boat speed increase
quiz.explanation: A yacht normally needs water flow over the rudder to respond.

quiz.prompt: After centering the helm, what happens?
options: The yacht returns automatically to north
The turn reduces and the yacht tends to maintain its new heading
quiz.explanation: The helm controls turning, not a selected compass heading.

sail-07.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Raise sails and build speed above 3 knots

practice.debrief: The sail force accelerated the boat; the rudder became useful as speed built.

sail-08.title: Hold a steady course
concepts: Steer by something far away, such as a headland or a cloud, and use the compass to check it. A distant mark shows a turn at once; the compass number lags behind and swings in waves.

A turning boat keeps turning after you center the helm, because it carries turning momentum, like a revolving door. So center the helm before you reach the new heading and let the boat glide onto it. If you wait until you are on the heading, you overshoot, correct back and zigzag. Small, early corrections give a straight track.

If you keep needing helm just to hold a straight course, the boat is telling you something. A yacht that keeps trying to turn toward the wind (weather helm) usually has too much sail up or is heeling too far; easing the mainsheet or reefing fixes it (Lesson 18). Keep a lookout as well: an accurately steered course can still lead into danger.
observe: Use short port or starboard inputs, then select Center.
Watch heading settle rather than keeping the helm over.
sail-08.mistake: Holding a large correction too long and oscillating from one side of the target to the other.

quiz.prompt: You are approaching your intended heading. What usually helps avoid overshoot?
options: Center the helm in good time
quiz.explanation: The boat has rotational response; reducing the correction early helps the turn settle.

quiz.prompt: Which is a complete steering routine?
options: Look away until the boat drifts
Look out, check heading, make a small correction, reassess
quiz.explanation: Steering and lookout must happen together.

sail-08.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 045° ±5°, above 2 knots, for 10 seconds
steps.hint: Port brings 060° down toward 045°. Center before you reach the target.

practice.debrief: A steady course requires small corrections and anticipation, not continuous large helm input.

sail-09.title: Find a beam reach
concepts: A point of sail is the angle between the bow and the wind, not a compass heading. Moving away from the wind: close hauled (about 40–50° off the wind, sails pulled in tight), close reach (about 60°), beam reach (90°, wind across the side), broad reach (about 135°, wind from behind the side) and run (about 180°, wind from behind).

Each point of sail has its own sail setting. A rough guide is that the sail sits at about half the wind angle: close hauled the boom is near the centerline, on a beam reach it is about halfway out, and on a run it is far out. You can be on any point of sail on either side of the wind: with wind from 315°, both 045° and 225° are beam reaches.

As the boat speeds up, the wind it feels swings forward, because its own motion adds a breeze from ahead (Lesson 17 explains this). So trim in a little as you accelerate. If the wind shifts, your point of sail changes even when your heading does not.
observe: Compare the bow marker with the direction of wind over water on the onboard display.
Notice that two different compass headings can give the same point of sail.
sail-09.mistake: Memorizing a compass heading as a point of sail when the wind direction may change.

quiz.prompt: What defines a beam reach?
quiz.explanation: Points of sail are relative to the wind.

quiz.prompt: If the wind shifts, can an unchanged heading produce a different point of sail?
quiz.explanation: A wind shift changes the angle between the bow and the wind.

sail-09.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a beam reach above 2 knots for 8 seconds

practice.debrief: You selected a course using the wind relationship, rather than the compass alone.

sail-10.title: Sail close hauled
concepts: How can a boat sail toward the wind? Air flowing around the curved sail makes a force, like the lift on an aircraft wing. Close hauled, that force points mostly sideways and only a little forward. The keel grips the water and resists the sideways part, so what is left drives the boat forward. That is why close hauled feels heeled and slower than a reach, and why the boat slides sideways a little (leeway).

Pointing higher is not always better. Steer too close to the wind (pinching) and the front of the sail starts to flap, drive drops and the boat slows; a slower keel grips less, so the boat also slips sideways more. A few degrees lower with good speed usually gets you upwind sooner. As you head up, trim in; if speed fades, bear away a little.

Telltales are short ribbons on both sides of the sail near its front edge. When both stream straight back, the air is flowing well. If the windward one (on the side the wind comes from) lifts or spins, you are too close to the wind or the sail is too far out: bear away a little or trim in. If the leeward one droops or spins, the sail is pulled in too far: ease it or head up a little.
observe: Start on a reach and steer nearer to the wind.
Trim inward as the wind angle decreases.
sail-10.mistake: Pinching: pointing too close to the wind and losing the speed that makes the boat and rudder work.

quiz.prompt: What is pinching?
options: Sailing too close to the wind and losing useful drive
Sailing with too much anchor chain
quiz.explanation: A slightly lower course may produce better upwind progress because it preserves speed.

quiz.prompt: Relative to a beam reach, a close-hauled mainsail is generally…
quiz.explanation: As you sail closer to the wind, the sail angle normally comes inward.

sail-10.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold 45°–58° off the wind above 2 knots

practice.debrief: You balanced pointing with boat speed. The simulator estimates leeway but does not assess reading physical telltales.

sail-11.title: Bear away to a broad reach
concepts: Bearing away turns the bow away from the wind and makes the wind angle larger. Ease the sheets as you turn, so each sail keeps its angle to the wind. If you leave them tight, the sail stalls: it heels the boat and pushes it sideways without making much speed.

As you turn downwind, the sail works less like a wing and more like a parachute: the wind mostly pushes on it from behind. The sideways force fades, so the boat heels less and feels calmer. On a broad reach, with the wind from behind the side, many boats are fast and comfortable.

Near dead downwind, watch the boom. If the wind comes round to the same side the boom is on (sailing by the lee), it can get behind the sail and throw the boom across in an accidental gybe. While learning, stay at about 150° off the wind or less and know which side the boom would swing to.
observe: Increase your angle to the wind, then ease the sheet.
Keep a margin from dead downwind while learning.
sail-11.mistake: Leaving the mainsheet tight after bearing away or losing track of which side the boom will move to.

quiz.prompt: What happens to wind angle when you bear away?
quiz.explanation: The bow moves farther away from the source of the wind.

quiz.prompt: What maneuver becomes a concern near dead downwind?
quiz.explanation: A small heading or wind change can take the wind across the stern and move the boom.

sail-11.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold a broad reach, 120°–150° off the wind

practice.debrief: You increased the wind angle and kept clear of an accidental stern crossing.

sail-12.title: Trim with feedback
concepts: Trim means setting the sail at the right angle to the wind. Too far out and the front edge flaps (luffing): air is not flowing across the sail properly, so it makes little drive. Too far in and the air breaks away from the back of the sail (stalling): the boat heels and slows but does not speed up. The best setting is just inside the point where luffing starts.

The classic method: ease the sheet slowly until the front of the sail starts to flap, then pull it in just until the flapping stops. Telltales make this easier to see. Repeat it after every course change or wind shift. “When in doubt, let it out”: a slightly eased sail costs little speed; an over-tight one costs a lot.

Change one thing at a time and give the boat time. Speed changes slowly (Lesson 7), so wait several seconds to see whether a change helped. In this app, a suggested sheet angle calculated from the apparent wind lets you check your result; on a real boat you trim by watching the sail’s front edge and the telltales.
observe: Leave the helm centered and change only the sheet.
Wait for speed to respond instead of making constant large changes.
sail-12.mistake: Changing heading and sheet simultaneously so you cannot tell which adjustment improved the boat.

quiz.prompt: For a useful trim comparison, which technique helps?
options: Hold a steady course and adjust one thing at a time
quiz.explanation: A stable course makes the effects of sheet changes easier to observe.

quiz.prompt: Both telltales are streaming. You pull the sheet in further and the leeward telltale starts to spin. What happened?
options: The sail is pulled in too far and starting to stall
quiz.explanation: Pulling in too far makes the airflow break away on the back (leeward) side. Ease the sheet until the leeward telltale streams again.

sail-12.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Hold efficient trim and speed for 10 seconds

practice.debrief: You used a controlled adjustment and allowed time for the speed response.

sail-13.title: Head up and bear away
concepts: Heading up turns toward the source of the wind; bearing away turns away from it. Port and starboard name turn direction relative to the boat, not whether you are heading up.
On one tack, a port turn may head up; on the opposite tack it may bear away. Always reason from the current wind direction, and trim to match: heading up means sheet in, bearing away means sheet out.
First sail at 50° off the wind, then at 110°. Settle each course before making the next change.
observe: Notice whether the wind angle grows or shrinks with each helm input.
Center the helm at each target, and adjust trim to the new point of sail.

quiz.prompt: Is a port turn always a turn toward the wind?
options: No; it depends on the tack and wind direction
quiz.explanation: The same helm direction changes the wind relationship differently on opposite tacks.

quiz.prompt: What should follow a substantial course change?
quiz.explanation: The new heading changes airflow and the situation around the boat.

sail-13.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Settle at 45°–55° off the wind
Bear away and settle at 105°–115°

practice.debrief: You changed your relationship to the wind in both directions and stabilized between turns.

sail-14.title: Make a controlled tack
concepts: A tack turns the bow through the wind, so the wind moves to the other side of the boat and the sails swap sides. From close hauled to close hauled, it is a turn of about 90°. Before you start, look for traffic, check sea room and warn the crew (“Ready about”).

Speed is what gets you through. Inside the no-go zone the sails flap and make no drive, so only the boat’s momentum carries the bow across. Start with good speed and turn steadily. Too slow, and the boat stops head to wind (in irons, Lesson 16). Too sharp, and the rudder, turned hard over, acts as a brake.

On a real yacht: put the helm over and call the turn (for example “Lee-ho”); as the headsail starts to flap, release its old sheet; as the bow passes the wind, pull in the new sheet on the other side; then center the helm on the new close-hauled course and retrim. Expect to lose some speed, and rebuild it before pointing high. In the app the sails swap sides automatically.
observe: Start with wind over the starboard side, then turn starboard through 315°.
Continue past the no-go zone, center the helm, and rebuild speed.
sail-14.mistake: Stopping the turn in the no-go zone, or calling a turn across the stern a tack.

quiz.prompt: Which part of the yacht crosses the wind during a tack?
quiz.explanation: A tack takes the bow through the source of the wind; a gybe takes the stern through it.

quiz.prompt: Before the turn, what is needed?
options: Lookout, sea room, preparation, and enough boat speed
All crew standing beneath the boom
quiz.explanation: Preparation and momentum help the boat complete the no-go-zone crossing.

sail-14.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Turn the bow through the wind and recover above 2 knots
steps.hint: Turn starboard through 315°, then continue to about 005° and center. Trim for the new course.

practice.debrief: The assessment recorded a bow crossing, a new tack, and recovered speed. Sheet transfer remains an on-water skill.

sail-15.title: Make a planned gybe
concepts: A gybe turns the stern through the wind. It is more dangerous than a tack because the sails stay full the whole time. In a tack the sails go slack as the bow passes the wind; in a gybe the wind gets behind the mainsail and throws the boom across the cockpit with force.

So you control the boom. Warn the crew (“Stand by to gybe”) and keep heads clear. Before the stern crosses the wind, pull the mainsheet in so the boom is near the center and has only a short distance to swing. Turn slowly; as the boom crosses, ease the sheet out smoothly on the new side and steady the helm so the boat does not swing up toward the wind.

Make it a small, deliberate turn from a broad reach on one side to a broad reach on the other. An accidental gybe, usually caused by sailing by the lee, is the dangerous version because nobody is ready. In the app the boom is animated, but its impact force is not modeled.
observe: Start at 160° with wind from 315°. Turn port toward and through 135°.
Settle near 110° and keep the wind well aft of the beam.
sail-15.mistake: Treating a gybe like an unannounced sharp turn with the mainsheet fully loose.

quiz.prompt: What is the principal gybe hazard for the crew?
options: The boom and mainsheet crossing the cockpit
quiz.explanation: Control the boom and keep people clear of its path.

quiz.prompt: What distinguishes a gybe from a tack?
options: The stern passes through the wind
The boat must use an engine
quiz.explanation: The wind crosses the stern during a gybe and the bow during a tack.

sail-15.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

steps.label: Cross the wind with the stern and settle on the new tack
steps.hint: Turn port through 135° and settle near 110°. Center the helm.

practice.debrief: You made the correct stern crossing. Real mainsheet control must be learned with supervision.

sail-16.title: Recover from loss of drive
concepts: In irons means stopped, or nearly stopped, pointing into the wind. The sails flap, so there is no drive, and as speed falls the rudder loses its grip on the water.
Avoid it by keeping speed through a tack and not pinching. If you notice it early, use the speed you still have: bear away promptly until the sails fill, then trim to rebuild drive.

A fully stopped boat needs another way to turn. On a real yacht the crew can hold the headsail out on one side (backing it) so the wind pushes the bow away, or let the boat drift backward and steer it round, remembering that steering works the opposite way going backward. Some crews use the engine. Backing sails is not modeled here, so this exercise starts with some speed left: use it before it runs out.
observe: Use the remaining way to turn away from 315°.
Do not wait until speed reaches zero before correcting.
sail-16.mistake: Expecting the rudder to rotate a fully stationary yacht without water flow.

quiz.prompt: Why should you act before all speed is lost?
options: Residual water flow gives steering authority
quiz.explanation: Use the remaining steerage to get outside the no-go zone.

quiz.prompt: The boat has stopped head to wind and starts to drift backward. What happens to the steering?
options: It works the opposite way: the same helm turns the bow the other way
It works exactly as when moving forward
quiz.explanation: Moving backward, water reaches the rudder from behind, so its effect reverses. Crews use this, together with a backed headsail, to turn the bow out of the no-go zone.

sail-17.title: True and apparent wind
concepts: Apparent wind is airflow relative to the yacht. Weather wind is relative to fixed ground; wind over water subtracts current from that air velocity. “True wind” may use either ground or water as its reference, so check the instrument convention.

As speed through water increases on a steady reach, apparent wind generally shifts forward relative to wind over water. Downwind, motion with the airflow can reduce apparent wind speed. When wind over water is calm, its direction is undefined, but a yacht moving through the water can still experience apparent airflow.

Compare Wind over water with Apparent wind on the onboard display. Use the wind over water to name your point of sail and the no-go zone; trim the sails to the apparent wind, because that is the air they actually feel. Telltales and sail shape always show the apparent wind directly.

A sail can work like an aircraft wing: deflecting airflow produces an aerodynamic force with a forward component and a sideways component. The keel, centreboard or underwater foils resist sideways motion. On a reach, a well-trimmed sail can still provide forward drive when boat speed exceeds true-wind speed. Acceleration ends when driving force balances resistance.

Efficient racing boats can therefore sail faster than the true wind. Light hulls and efficient sails help; hydrofoils can lift the hull clear of the water and reduce resistance further. The energy comes from wind moving relative to the water. Apparent wind describes the airflow at the moving sail; boat motion creates no extra energy. An ordinary cruising yacht may have too much resistance to exceed wind speed.

For a worked example, assume no current or leeway: a racing boat travels north at 30 knots while a 20-knot wind blows from the west. The two velocities are perpendicular. Apparent wind speed is √(20² + 30²) ≈ 36.1 knots, arriving about 34° to port of the bow. This calculates the airflow for an assumed boat speed; it does not prove that every boat can reach 30 knots. Sailing straight downwind at wind speed instead removes the apparent airflow in this simple case.

Try it in Challenges → Apparent Wind Lab: record the wind with the sails down, then on a beam reach, then on a broad reach. On the beam reach the apparent wind gets stronger and moves forward as speed builds; on the broad reach it gets weaker.
observe: Imagine riding a bicycle in still air: you feel wind from ahead.
Compare the apparent wind display as speed increases on a steady course.
sail-17.mistake: Assuming true and apparent wind have identical direction and speed while the yacht is moving.

quiz.prompt: What wind does a moving sail actually experience?
quiz.explanation: Sails interact with airflow relative to the moving yacht.

quiz.prompt: You speed up on a steady beam reach. What happens to the apparent wind?
options: It moves forward and gets stronger
It moves aft and gets weaker
quiz.explanation: The boat’s own motion adds a breeze from ahead. Combined with the true wind, the apparent wind swings toward the bow and strengthens, so you trim in a little.

quiz.prompt: Why can an efficient racing boat sail faster than the true wind on a reach?
options: Boat motion creates an unlimited energy supply
Sail lift can still provide forward drive greater than resistance
Every sailboat automatically matches apparent wind speed
quiz.explanation: The sail interacts with apparent airflow while underwater surfaces resist sideways motion. With sufficiently low resistance, useful forward drive can remain above true-wind speed. Energy still comes from wind relative to water.

quiz.prompt: With no current or leeway, a boat travels at 30 knots perpendicular to a 20-knot true wind. What apparent wind speed does it experience?
quiz.explanation: Perpendicular velocities combine as √(20² + 30²) ≈ 36.1 knots. Adding or subtracting the speeds directly only applies to collinear motion; this example assumes the boat has reached 30 knots.

sail-18.title: Reef before you need to
concepts: Wind force grows with the square of wind speed: 20 knots pushes about four times as hard as 10 knots, not twice. So a moderate rise in wind makes a big rise in the force heeling the boat and loading the rig. A reef makes the mainsail smaller and lower, so the force is smaller and acts lower down, which means less heel.

Too much heel does not make a boat faster. The hull slips sideways more, the rudder grips less, and the boat keeps trying to turn into the wind (weather helm). Signs that it is time to reef: heavy steering, the boat rounding up toward the wind in gusts, and water along the side deck. “Reef when you first think about it”: it is far easier before the wind builds than during it.

There is no single wind speed for reefing: it depends on the boat, the crew, the gusts and the sea. Compare the heel and the helm before and after a reef on the same course. The app’s Reef control shortens the main in one step; on a real boat it means handling the halyard and reefing lines under load, with the crew working together.
observe: Observe heel and speed in the exercise’s 22-knot breeze.
Select Reef, keep the boat on a reach, and compare its response.
sail-18.mistake: Waiting until the crew are overloaded or using a fixed wind threshold without considering the boat.

quiz.prompt: What is a sound reason to reef early?
options: Increasing difficulty keeping the yacht controlled
Every yacht always reefs at exactly 20 knots
quiz.explanation: Reefing is a control decision based on boat, crew, and conditions.

quiz.prompt: The wind rises from 10 to 20 knots. Roughly how much harder does it push on the sails?
quiz.explanation: Wind force grows with the square of wind speed: 2 × 2 = 4. That is why reefing decisions come earlier than many beginners expect.

sail-19.title: Reduce power deliberately
concepts: A sailing yacht has no brakes. When you take power out of the sails, the boat keeps moving on its momentum and slows only as water drag works on it; a heavy boat can glide a long way. Plan the stop early and leave sea room.

Ways to take power out, from quickest to most complete: ease the sheets until the sails flap, so they stop working as wings; head up toward the wind, which reduces the angle and the drive; lower the sails, which removes drive completely. As the boat slows, the rudder grips less, so steering becomes slow and weak.

On a real yacht you can also heave to: set the sails to work against each other so the boat almost stops and sits quietly. That is not modeled here. In this exercise, lower the sails and wait until speed is below 1 knot. The anchor is not a brake.
observe: Compare the speed before and after lowering sails.
Notice the delay and the reduction in rudder authority.
sail-19.mistake: Dropping an anchor at speed as a routine way to stop.

quiz.prompt: What remains after you lower the sails?
quiz.explanation: The boat continues to move until drag reduces its speed.

quiz.prompt: Why leave room when slowing down?
options: Stopping distance and declining steerage need to be anticipated
The compass becomes unreliable at low speed
quiz.explanation: Plan your speed reduction early enough to remain in control.

Coast below 1 knot without anchoring

sail-20.title: Choose a weather limit
concepts: Read a marine forecast for the whole intended trip and a margin beyond it. Consider mean wind, gusts, direction changes, sea state, visibility, temperature, tides, and local effects.

Wind against current builds steep, short waves: the current squeezes the waves together, so they become taller and closer and can break. A lee shore is a coast the wind is blowing toward. It is dangerous because if anything fails, such as the engine, a sail or the rudder, the wind pushes you onto it. An offshore wind feels calm near the coast but can make it hard to get back.

Set your go/no-go limits and escape options before you leave: what change would make you shorten the trip, and where you would go instead. The simulator’s wind is steady and its current does not change, so practice this judgment here as planning; real weather changes.
observe: For a novice crew, decide what change would make you shorten or cancel a trip.
Name a sheltered alternative and a return deadline.
sail-20.mistake: Treating a low average wind speed as proof that the entire trip will be safe.

quiz.prompt: The average wind is manageable but the forecast includes strong gusts and worsening visibility. What is appropriate?
options: Depart because only average speed matters
Reassess the trip against crew ability and safe alternatives
quiz.explanation: The entire forecast and its trend matter, not one number.

quiz.prompt: Strong wind is forecast to blow onto the coast you plan to follow. Why is that a concern?
options: It is a lee shore: if something fails, the wind pushes you toward land
It always makes the sea calmer
quiz.explanation: With wind blowing onto the shore you have little room to recover from a failure. Choose a route with more sea room or change the plan.

sail-21.title: Read a practice chart
concepts: A chart is a planning tool, not a picture to follow blindly. Check scale, orientation, depth information, hazards, marks, and the source and currency of the chart.

Depths are numbers, usually in metres, and lines called contours join places of equal depth. Shallower water is usually shaded blue, areas that dry at low tide are green, and land is buff or yellow. Measure distance on the latitude scale at the side of the chart: one minute of latitude is one nautical mile.

Buoys tell you what to do. Lateral marks show the two sides of a channel, and each is passed on a set side; cardinal marks show on which side of a danger the safe water lies. Which color goes on which side depends on the region (IALA A or B), so check before you sail. In this app the amber buoys are only practice targets.
observe: Open the chart. Locate north, your position, and the next mark.
Identify land you must keep clear of along the intended route.
sail-21.mistake: Assuming a screen showing your position is a complete and current navigational chart.

quiz.prompt: On a chart, what does one minute of latitude on the side scale measure?
quiz.explanation: Distance is measured on the latitude scale at the side of the chart, level with your position. The longitude scale along the top and bottom changes with latitude, so it is not used for distance.

quiz.prompt: Which should a real chart check include?
options: Scale, source, currency, depths, hazards, and local conventions
quiz.explanation: Charts need interpretation and context to support safe navigation.

sail-22.title: Steer toward a waypoint
concepts: A bearing is the direction from your position to a target. Decide whether the direct track is safe and sailable before following it.
A direct bearing may point into the no-go zone or cross land. In those cases, plan a different route rather than forcing the bow toward the target.

Where the bow points is not always where the boat goes. Current and leeway push you sideways, so aim a little up-current of the mark. Check the bearing to the mark now and then: if it keeps changing while you hold your heading, you are being pushed off the line. In this exercise, pass within 35 metres of buoy 1.
observe: Open the chart before changing course.
Aim toward buoy 1, then check progress and depth regularly.
sail-22.mistake: Fixating on the target and ignoring land, traffic, or the wind angle.

quiz.prompt: Your waypoint lies directly upwind. What is required?
options: Plan a sailable route using tacks
Hold the bow in the no-go zone indefinitely
Increase the compass reading until the wind changes
quiz.explanation: You may need multiple legs to make progress toward an upwind destination.

quiz.prompt: Is the direct bearing always a safe course?
options: Only if the waypoint is visible
No; check hazards, depth, wind, and traffic
quiz.explanation: A bearing describes direction, not safety.

Reach buoy 1 with at least 3 m depth

sail-23.title: Estimate distance and time
concepts: For a first estimate, distance equals speed multiplied by time. At 4 knots, a 3-nautical-mile leg takes 45 minutes if speed remains constant and there is no current.
Dead reckoning advances an earlier position using course, speed, and time. Real estimates also account for current, leeway, and uncertainty; a fix from observations checks the estimate.
Record assumptions and update the estimate as conditions change. Do not confuse a precise-looking number with an accurate prediction.
observe: Compute the time for 3 nautical miles at 4 knots before checking the answer.
Describe one reason the actual arrival time might differ.
sail-23.mistake: Mixing minutes and hours or ignoring current and changing boat speed.

quiz.prompt: At 4 knots, how long is a 3-nautical-mile leg without current?
quiz.explanation: 3 ÷ 4 hours = 0.75 hour = 45 minutes.

quiz.prompt: What checks an estimated position?
options: Assuming the log cannot be wrong
An independent position observation or fix
quiz.explanation: An estimate needs verification and an allowance for uncertainty.

sail-24.title: Sail a short passage
concepts: Break a route into manageable legs with clear targets, hazards, and a plan for the next turn. Keep a lookout before altering course at a mark.
This exercise runs from south of buoy 1 to buoy 1, then buoy 2. The wind makes both direct legs sailable, but you still need to turn and retrim.
Keep at least 3 metres of modeled water depth. Grounding invalidates the attempt and requires a restart; passing the marks alone is not sufficient.
observe: Study both legs before setting off.
At buoy 1, look toward buoy 2 and prepare the course change.
sail-24.mistake: Reaching a waypoint without planning what happens immediately afterward.

quiz.prompt: When should the next leg be considered?
options: Only after leaving the chart behind
Before arriving at the turning point
Never; the yacht follows marks automatically
quiz.explanation: Anticipation leaves time for lookout, crew preparation, and safe course changes.

quiz.prompt: You passed the marks but ran aground. Was the passage successful?
options: No; avoiding hazards is part of the task
Yes, if the speed was high
quiz.explanation: A completed route is not a safe route if essential margins were lost.

sail-25.title: Keep an effective lookout
concepts: A proper lookout uses sight, hearing, and appropriate available means. Scan ahead, astern, and to both sides; the sails and structures can hide other craft.

Why a steady bearing means danger: two boats on straight courses that will meet stay at the same angle to each other all the way to the meeting point. So if another vessel stays on the same compass bearing, or stays lined up with the same part of your boat, while it gets closer, you are on a collision course. Check early and repeatedly, and act rather than wait for certainty.
Electronic aids support the lookout; they do not replace it. This world has static moored yachts and does not assess realistic traffic detection.
observe: Use the camera to scan the side hidden by the headsail.
Explain how you would share lookout duties with a real crew.
sail-25.mistake: Looking only ahead or only at the chartplotter.

quiz.prompt: A nearby vessel stays at a nearly constant bearing while the distance closes. What might that indicate?
options: No risk because it is not changing direction on the window
A guarantee that it will pass astern
quiz.explanation: Constant bearing with decreasing range is a classic warning; act early based on the full situation.

quiz.prompt: Can a chartplotter replace sight and hearing?
quiz.explanation: Use all appropriate available means and keep an outside lookout.

sail-25.transfer: Practice this with a qualified instructor aboard a real yacht. The simulator cannot reproduce crew coordination, loads, or all vessel behavior.

sail-26.title: Reason through encounters
concepts: The rules decide in advance who turns away (gives way) and who holds course (stands on), so two boats do not both turn the same way. For two sailing vessels: on different tacks, the port-tack boat keeps clear; on the same tack, the windward boat keeps clear, because it can usually bear away more easily. Lesson 46 covers this in full.

An overtaking vessel keeps clear. Other vessel responsibilities, narrow channels, traffic schemes, restricted visibility, and local rules can change the analysis. Do not reduce the rules to “sail always wins.”
A stand-on vessel still has responsibilities and must act when needed to avoid collision. Learn the full applicable collision regulations and local requirements before sailing.
observe: Identify the windward side of each vessel before deciding its tack.
State the assumptions before applying a simplified crossing rule.
sail-26.mistake: Treating stand-on status as permission to ignore developing collision risk.

quiz.prompt: In a basic two-sailing-vessel encounter on different tacks, which normally keeps clear?
quiz.explanation: Under the basic sailing-vessel rule, port tack keeps clear of starboard tack, subject to the full situation and other applicable rules.

quiz.prompt: Does a stand-on vessel have no further responsibility?
options: No; it must continue monitoring and act as required to avoid collision
Yes; it can close its eyes
Yes; the other vessel accepts all responsibility
quiz.explanation: Collision avoidance is an ongoing duty. The complete rules specify stand-on actions and responsibilities.

sail-27.title: Lights, marks, and signals
concepts: Navigation lights show a vessel’s direction and what it is doing. Red is on the port side, green on starboard and white at the stern. See both red and green, and the vessel is heading straight at you; red only, you see its port side; green only, its starboard side; white only, you are looking at its stern.

In the international maneuvering-signal context, one short blast means altering course to starboard, two to port, and three operating astern propulsion. Restricted-visibility signals are a different system; local or inland rules may differ.
Lesson 50 covers the full lights, shapes and sound signals. Rules can differ in inland or local waters, so check the rules for where you sail before night or restricted-visibility operation.
observe: Identify the red port light and green starboard light on the yacht.
Distinguish an action signal from a signal used in restricted visibility.
sail-27.mistake: Assuming one memorized signal applies in every jurisdiction and situation.

quiz.prompt: Which side normally carries the red sidelight?
quiz.explanation: The port sidelight is red; starboard is green.

quiz.prompt: In the stated international maneuvering-signal context, two short blasts indicate…
quiz.explanation: Two short blasts mean altering course to port in that context; do not generalize without checking the applicable rules.

sail-28.title: Make a passage decision
concepts: A passage plan includes the crew, forecast, route, hazards, tidal constraints, daylight, safe havens, communications, and a latest turn-back time.
Good seamanship includes changing or abandoning the plan when its assumptions fail. Do not let a fixed arrival promise outweigh safety margins.
Scenario: you have a novice crew, fading daylight, a forecast wind increase, and an exposed destination. A nearby sheltered alternative is available.
observe: Name the factors that make the original destination less suitable.
Choose a conservative alternative and tell the crew why.
sail-28.mistake: Continuing because the destination was promised before conditions changed.

quiz.prompt: For the stated scenario, which is the sounder decision?
options: Press on to preserve the schedule
Ask the least experienced crew member to decide alone
Reassess and favor the sheltered alternative or an early return
quiz.explanation: Rising exposure and shrinking margins support a conservative change of plan.

quiz.prompt: Which makes an abort plan useful?
options: Clear decision points and viable alternatives
Leaving every decision until the last minute
A promise never to change course
quiz.explanation: Specific triggers and alternatives help avoid rushed decisions under pressure.

sail-29.title: Plan a docking approach
concepts: Docking combines wind, current, propeller effects, boat momentum, and crew coordination. Prepare fenders and lines, assign roles, choose an approach, and keep an escape route.

Approach into the wind or the current where you can: it slows you down, so you can arrive slowly while water still flows past the rudder for steering. Arrive at the slowest speed that still lets you steer, the speed you would be willing to touch the dock at. Never use a hand or foot to stop the boat.

Two effects catch beginners. In reverse, the propeller pulls the stern to one side (prop walk), so the boat will not back straight at first. And at low speed the wind pushes the high bow away from the dock. Plan for both, and keep a way out. Prop walk and dock lines are not modeled in the app, so docking is taught here as planning.
observe: Describe your approach, crew jobs, and go-around plan before moving.
Explain why wind and current change a safe approach.
sail-29.mistake: Relying on crew to jump ashore or physically catch the yacht.

quiz.prompt: If the approach becomes unstable, what should the preplanned option be?
options: Ask someone to fend off with a foot
Abort and make a controlled new approach if safe
Add speed to get it over with
quiz.explanation: An escape plan is part of preparation; avoid trapping the boat or crew in an unrecoverable maneuver.

quiz.prompt: Why approach a berth heading into the wind or current when you can?
options: It makes the boat go faster
It slows the boat while water still flows past the rudder
quiz.explanation: The wind or current acts as a brake, so you can come in slowly and still steer. With them behind you, the boat keeps being pushed on.

sail-30.title: Choose an anchorage
concepts: Choose shelter, suitable holding ground, adequate depth throughout the tidal range, and room to swing without reaching hazards or neighboring vessels.

An anchor holds best when it is pulled flat along the seabed, because then it digs in. With a short rode the pull comes from above and lifts the anchor out. That is why you let out several times the depth: the extra length, and the weight of chain, keep the pull flat and soften jerks from waves. Use more in strong wind. Scope is rode length divided by the height from bow roller to seabed.

Example for arithmetic only: at 5 m water depth and a roller 1 m above water, an assumed 5:1 ratio gives 30 m of rode. This calculation is not a deployment prescription. Add tidal changes and assess swing room.
observe: Sketch the expected swing circle and nearby hazards.
Include roller height in the example’s vertical distance.
sail-30.mistake: Multiplying charted depth alone or assuming an anchor always holds once it touches bottom.

quiz.prompt: Under the stated example assumptions, how much rode corresponds to 5:1?
quiz.explanation: The vertical distance is 5 + 1 = 6 m. Five times 6 m is 30 m, before other real-world considerations.

quiz.prompt: What must an anchorage plan consider beyond depth?
options: Only the distance to a café
Shelter, holding ground, tide, swing room, and hazards
quiz.explanation: Depth alone does not establish a suitable or safe anchorage.

sail-31.title: Stop, then anchor
concepts: Approach slowly, heading into the wind (or the current, whichever affects the boat more), so the boat comes to a stop on its own. Lower the anchor to the seabed once the boat has stopped. Then let the wind push the boat backward as you pay out rode, so the chain lies along the bottom instead of piling on top of the anchor.

When enough rode is out, set the anchor by pulling on it gently, often with a little engine astern. Check that it holds: pick two objects ashore that line up, and watch whether they stay lined up. Keep checking over time, especially when the wind changes.

In this exercise: lower the sails and coast below 0.8 knots with the anchor up. Set a 45 m rode target and run the windlass; it pays out over time and stops at the target. Wait for 45 m actually paid out, the windlass stopped, and ground speed below 0.2 knots. Deploying early ends the attempt.
observe: Reduce sail power well before the intended stopping point.
Wait for speed to fall before using the anchor control.
sail-31.mistake: Deploying the anchor at speed instead of completing a controlled approach.

quiz.prompt: What is the correct sequence in this exercise?
options: Anchor at full speed, then lower sails
Lower sails, slow with anchor up, then anchor
quiz.explanation: The exercise checks anticipation and sequencing, not the anchor’s holding ability.

quiz.prompt: Why let the boat drift back while paying out rode?
options: So the rode lies along the seabed instead of piling on the anchor
So the anchor stays off the bottom
quiz.explanation: Rode piled on top of the anchor can foul it. Letting the boat fall back lays the rode out, so the pull on the anchor stays flat.

sail-32.title: Prepare to leave
concepts: Before departure, recheck the surrounding area, intended route, conditions, and crew readiness. Make sure lines and equipment are secure and everyone knows what happens next.

To lift the anchor, bring the boat to it rather than pulling the boat with the rode. Motor or sail slowly toward the anchor while the crew brings in the slack. When the rode is straight up and down, the pull is vertical and the anchor breaks out of the seabed easily. The windlass lifts the rode; it is not for towing the boat.

Once the anchor leaves the bottom you are drifting, so get steerage quickly by engine or sail. In this exercise the bow starts above the anchor. Select Weigh anchor and wait until it is fully stowed, then raise the sails and settle on a steady reach. If the rode goes tight, retrieval pauses.
observe: Confirm the wind and your intended course before releasing the hold.
Restore sail power, gain steerage, and make a controlled departure.
sail-32.mistake: Releasing the boat before having a clear plan and adequate room.

quiz.prompt: What belongs before releasing the boat?
options: Crew briefing, lookout, and a clear plan
Looking at the route only after leaving
quiz.explanation: Preparation should precede the point at which the vessel is free to move.

quiz.prompt: When does an anchor break out of the seabed most easily?
options: When the rode is pulled flat along the bottom
When the rode is straight up and down above it
When the boat moves away fast
quiz.explanation: A vertical pull lifts the anchor’s point out. A flat pull is what makes it dig in, which is why you bring the boat over the anchor first.
